opus-5.5.text:
I think Abhinav is a really interesting figure to place within the CMU lineage, because CMU robotics historically has been very grounded in engineering rigor: careful modeling, planning, control, building systems that actually work on real hardware. That tradition runs deep, from the field robotics work to manipulation and motion planning.

What Abhinav brought, coming more from the computer vision side, was a different bet: that data at scale could be the main driver of progress in robotics, the way it had been in vision. Early on, that was not an obvious position. A lot of people felt robotics was fundamentally different, that you couldn't just collect lots of data and expect structure to emerge, because the physical world is expensive, slow, and unforgiving. Abhinav's group pushed on exactly that, doing things like large-scale self-supervised grasping, letting robots collect their own experience, and trying to learn from passive data like videos of humans.

So in a sense the approach is both continuous with and a departure from the CMU tradition. It's continuous in that there's still a strong emphasis on real robots and real-world experiments. It's not simulation-only or purely theoretical. But it's a departure in the philosophy of where the knowledge should come from. Instead of the engineer encoding the structure, the hope is that the data reveals it.

Looking back now, with all the excitement around robot foundation models and large-scale data collection, a lot of that early intuition looks quite prescient. At the same time, I think the field has also learned that data alone isn't the whole story. How you collect it, what embodiment it comes from, and how you combine it with good inductive biases still matters a lot. So in my view the most productive place to be is somewhere between those two traditions, and CMU is interesting precisely because it housed both of them.

fable-5.1.text:
Abhinav is very much a product of that CMU tradition, but he also pushed against it in an interesting way. CMU robotics has always been grounded in the physical world, in getting real systems to actually work, going back to people like Takeo Kanade and the Robotics Institute's whole engineering ethos. Abhinav came in from the vision side, and I think his real contribution was insisting that perception and action had to be learned together, not designed separately and then bolted on.

When he started his lab, a lot of people in robotics were still skeptical of large-scale data-driven learning. The classical view was that you model the dynamics, you plan, you control. Abhinav's bet was closer to what had already happened in computer vision: that if you collect enough interaction data, the representations you need will emerge. The work with robots grasping objects tens of thousands of times, learning from their own failures, was a very CMU thing to do in that it was hands-on and physical, but a very un-CMU thing in that it trusted scale over structure.

I also think he brought a certain intellectual restlessness. He wasn't satisfied with one benchmark or one task. He kept asking what the equivalent of ImageNet for robotics would be, whether it was self-supervision, curiosity, or physical interaction as a source of signal. That question is still open, honestly, but he framed it early and trained a lot of students who carried it forward, into Meta, into startups, into Skild. So I'd say he sits in the lineage, but as one of the people who turned it from a mostly engineering culture toward a learning culture.
